title: Citizenship and Community Skills
summary: Understand rights and responsibilities, how local communities are run, and how to take part. Practise organising projects, debating respectfully and checking information.
audience: Secondary and university students and young people

body.p: A right is something every person is entitled to, such as being treated fairly, being safe from harm, and getting an education. A responsibility is something you are expected to do in return, such as respecting other people's rights and following fair rules. Rights and responsibilities go together. If my right to speak is protected, your right to speak and be heard is protected as well, and I have a duty not to silence you.

In most countries, rights are written down in a constitution, in laws, and in international agreements that countries have signed. The details differ between Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Spain, Canada and the others, so it is important to look up your own country's rules from official sources, such as your government website, a national human rights body or a legal aid organisation. This course teaches the ideas, not the exact legal wording.

body.h: Rights and responsibilities side by side

list: Right to education, responsibility to attend, try your best and respect teachers and classmates.
Right to express your opinion, responsibility to do so without threats, insults or lies about others.
Right to be safe, responsibility not to bully or harm others, and to report danger.
Right to privacy, responsibility to respect other people's privacy, including photos and messages.
Right to fair treatment, responsibility to treat others fairly whatever their background.

body.h: Worked scenario: the school notice board

body.p: A student posts an angry message on the class group chat naming a teacher and making an untrue claim. The student believes freedom of speech allows this. Think it through: speaking up about a real problem is a right, but spreading a false accusation harms someone else's reputation and can break school rules or the law. A better action is to raise the concern with the head teacher or student council with facts. Using a right well means thinking about its effect on others.

body.tip: When you feel your rights have been ignored, write down what happened, when, and who was involved. Clear facts make it easier for any authority or adviser to help you.

lessons.title: How communities and local government work

body.p: Every community has several layers of decision-making. There is the household, the school or workplace, the neighbourhood, and then local government such as a town council, municipality, district or county, and finally regional and national government. Different countries name these layers differently and give them different powers, so your first task is to learn your own system.

list: Waste collection, drainage and local roads.
Markets, street lighting and some public spaces.
Local licences and permits for small businesses and events.
Some health clinics, schools or libraries, depending on the country.
Planning and building rules for the area.

body.p: Other tasks, such as defence, currency or national exams, usually belong to national government. In some places traditional or community leaders also play important roles, such as settling local disagreements or organising communal work.

body.h: Finding out how your own system works

steps: Search for the official website of your local council, municipality or district office.
Find out who your local representative or leader is and how to contact them.
Look for when public meetings are held and whether residents can attend.
Check what services the office provides and how to apply for them.
Ask a teacher, librarian or community adult if you cannot find information online.

body.p: A drain near a school in a busy market area is blocked, and the street floods when it rains. Who should be told? Ask which body in your area manages drainage. It may be the local council works office or an environmental health team. A good report names the location, shows a photo, explains the risk and asks for a specific action. Residents who understand the structure get answers more quickly than those who complain without knowing where to go.

body.tip: Write down the names and contact details of three local offices that matter to you, such as the council, the health clinic and the police station.

body.p: Voting is a way for members of a group to make a shared choice. It can be a school council election, a village meeting, a student union election or a national election. Voting works best when people understand the choices, the rules are fair, and the count is open. This lesson explains the idea in a non-partisan way. It does not tell you whom to vote for.

list: It gives people a say in decisions that affect them, such as services and rules.
It allows peaceful change of leaders without violence.
It holds leaders to account because they must face the voters.
Low participation means a smaller group decides for everyone.

body.p: In a student union election, 800 students are registered to vote and 520 actually vote. Turnout is 520 divided by 800, multiplied by 100, which is 65 percent. That means 280 students did not vote, so their views were not counted. Suppose three candidates receive 210, 180 and 130 votes. The total is 520. Candidate A has the most votes, but 261 would be needed for an absolute majority (more than half). Some systems simply give the win to the highest number of votes, called plurality. Others require a majority or a second round. Learn which system your country and your institutions use.

steps: Check the eligibility rules and registration deadlines from the official election body.
Read about each option from several sources and compare their plans with facts.
Ask whether promises are realistic, and who would pay and how.
Keep your vote private and never sell or trade it. Pressure or payment for votes is wrong and often illegal.
Respect the result and use peaceful, lawful routes if you have a complaint.

body.tip: Practise democratic habits early: run a fair class election with a clear rule for counting and a neutral person who checks the count.

lessons.title: Volunteering and organising a community project

body.p: Volunteering means giving time freely to help others or improve your community. It builds skills such as teamwork, communication and planning, and it shows employers and universities that you take responsibility. Good volunteering listens first. Ask the community what it needs rather than assuming.

steps: Identify a real need by talking to residents, leaders or teachers.
Set one clear goal and a date, for example: repaint the school wall in one Saturday.
Ask for permission from the owner of the place and from the relevant authority.
Make a team with roles: leader, treasurer, safety officer, communications and recorder.
Write a simple budget and plan how to get what you need, through donations, contributions or local businesses.
Do the work safely and thank everyone.
Review what worked and write it down for the next team.

body.p: A youth club plans to paint a wall mural. 25 volunteers will work 3 hours each, so total volunteer time is 25 x 3 = 75 hours. The costs are paint 4500, brushes and rollers 1500, refreshments 2000 and printing posters 1000, which adds to 9000 currency units. The club collects 6000 from members and local shops, so there is a gap of 9000-6000 = 3000 units. The group decides to ask two shops for donated paint rather than cash, and the budget is balanced. Writing the budget first exposed the gap before work started.

list: Get written parental or school permission for volunteers under 18.
Do a short risk check: weather, traffic, tools, drinking water.
Keep honest records of money received and spent, and share them openly.
Include people of different backgrounds and abilities.
Never ask volunteers to do work that needs trained professionals.

body.tip: A good volunteer project solves a problem and leaves people more able to do it themselves next time.

body.p: In any community, people see things differently. Disagreement is normal and can lead to better ideas, if it is handled well. A respectful debate is about testing ideas, not defeating a person. You can disagree strongly and still treat the other person with dignity.

list: Listen fully before replying. Try to repeat the other person's point in your own words.
Ask questions to understand: What makes you think so? Can you give an example?
Separate the person from the idea. Say 'I disagree with that point', not 'you are stupid'.
Use evidence and say where it comes from.
Admit what you do not know, and change your mind when the evidence is good.
Attacking the person rather than the argument.
Making the other side's view sound silly, so that it is easy to defeat.
Presenting only two choices when more exist.
Claiming that something is true because 'everyone says so'.
Shouting or interrupting.

body.p: Two students argue about whether the school should allow a simpler uniform to cut costs for families. One says, 'You only think that because you are lazy.' This attacks the person. A stronger reply is, 'I understand the cost worry. What would happen to the school's identity and to students who already have the uniform?' Both students then look at facts: price of items, how many families struggle, and alternatives such as a second-hand uniform shop. They may not agree fully, but they end with a shared list of options for the head teacher.

body.tip: If a discussion becomes heated, pause, take a breath, and suggest returning to it later. A calm ending protects the relationship.

lessons.title: Media and misinformation on public issues

body.p: Today news and opinion reach you through radio, television, newspapers, websites and, above all, social media and messaging groups. Information that is false can spread faster than the truth, especially when it makes people angry or afraid. Misinformation is false information shared without meaning harm. Disinformation is false information shared on purpose to mislead. Both can affect health, safety and public life.

body.h: A quick check before you share

steps: Stop and notice your feelings. A message designed to make you furious or scared deserves extra care.
Who made this? Is there a named author, organisation, date and place?
What is the evidence? Look for original documents, data or direct quotes.
Do other reliable sources report the same thing? Search for the main claim.
Check images and videos. Old photos are often reused for new events. A reverse image search can help.
If you cannot verify it, do not share it.

body.p: A message in a family group says that a local market will be closed by the council from tomorrow and everyone must collect their goods tonight. It has no name, no date and no link, and ends with 'forward to 10 people'. Check the council's official page or phone line, and ask neighbours who work in the market. If the council has not said it, it is likely false. Sharing it could cause panic and loss. Replying kindly with the verified fact, such as 'The council website shows no announcement, please check before forwarding', helps the group.

list: A fact can be checked, for example the date of a public meeting.
An opinion is a view, for example 'the meeting was boring'.
Headlines may exaggerate. Read beyond them.
Be aware of your own bias: we often believe what agrees with us.

body.tip: Follow a mix of reliable sources, including local ones, and learn how to find the original source of a claim.

lessons.title: Reporting problems, consumer rights and staying safe online

body.p: Active citizens know where to take a problem. If a street light is broken, report it to the local authority. If a crime has happened, contact the police. If a service such as water or electricity is failing, contact the provider and, if needed, the regulator. If a shop has sold a faulty product, begin with the seller. Each country has different offices, so look up yours in advance.

body.h: How to make a good report

steps: State what happened, where and when, in clear short sentences.
Add evidence: photos, receipts, reference numbers, names of people you spoke to.
Say what you want done.
Keep a copy and note the date you sent it.
Follow up politely after a reasonable time and move to the next level if there is no reply.

body.p: In most places consumers can expect goods to be safe, to match their description and to work as they should. They can expect honest prices and clear information. If an item is faulty, there is usually a route for a repair, replacement or refund. Rules differ, so check your national consumer body. Always keep your receipt. Worked example: Kemi buys 4 phone cases at 2500 units each, total 10000 units. One has a broken clip and the seller refuses help. Kemi shows the receipt, explains the fault politely and asks for a replacement or a refund of 2500 units for that item. If the seller refuses, she writes to the shop manager and then to the local consumer office. In another case, a coat marked 8000 units is sold at 15 percent off, so the price is 8000 x 0.85 = 6800 units. Always check that the final price on the receipt matches what was advertised.

list: Use strong passwords that are long and unique, and turn on two-step verification where offered.
Length helps: a password with only 4 lowercase letters has 456976 possible combinations, which a computer can try quickly, while longer passwords with mixed characters are far harder to guess.
Think before you post. Photos, locations and school details can be copied and used by others.
Do not share one-time codes or PINs. Real banks and mobile money providers do not ask for them.
Be suspicious of offers that seem too good or messages that rush you.
Block and report bullies or scammers, and tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong. Save evidence first.

body.tip: Treat people online as you would face to face. Your digital footprint is part of your reputation as a citizen.

quiz.q: A student has the right to express opinions. Which action also respects the responsibility that goes with that right?
options: Posting a false accusation about a teacher in a group chat to pressure the school
Raising a concern about a teacher, with facts, through the proper school channel
Shouting down classmates who disagree until they stop giving their own views
Anonymously sending threats to the person so that they will change their behaviour

quiz.q: Where should you first look to learn which office handles drainage in your area?
options: A rumour passed on by a friend of a friend who lives near the area
A social media post with no author, which has been shared many times
The official website or office of your local council or municipality
The nearest shop sign or a notice that someone stuck on a wall

quiz.q: A street drain floods near a school. Which report is most likely to get action?
options: A general complaint posted online that says the roads in the area are bad and nobody cares
A message to a national office complaining about every local problem in the whole town at once
Waiting for someone else to report it, since a person living closer is more likely to know who to tell
A message with the exact location, a photo, the risk and a clear request, sent to the correct office

quiz.q: 800 students are registered and 520 vote. What is the turnout?
options: 65 percent
35 percent
153.85 percent
52 percent

quiz.q: Three candidates get 210, 180 and 130 votes. What is the total number of votes, and how many would be needed for more than half?
options: Total 520; 260 needed
Total 390; 261 needed
Total 520; 261 needed
Total 520; 210 needed

quiz.q: A person offers you money in return for your vote. What is the right response?
options: Accept the money but vote as you wish, since nobody can prove how you voted
Sell your vote to whichever person offers you the highest amount of money
Offer the same deal to your friends so that more people get paid for voting
Refuse the offer, keep your vote private and report it if you can safely do so

quiz.q: A club has 25 volunteers for 3 hours each. How many volunteer hours is that?
options: 28 hours
75 hours
150 hours
25 hours

quiz.q: A project costs: paint 4500, brushes 1500, refreshments 2000, posters 1000. The club has raised 6000. How much more is needed?
options: 3000 units
9000 units
6000 units
4000 units

quiz.q: Before starting a clean-up of a private compound, the team has not asked the owner. What is the best step?
options: Start anyway, since the cause is good and the owner will probably be pleased
Tell the owner afterwards, once the work has been done and the area is clean
Ask the owner only if a problem comes up or someone complains about the work
Pause the clean-up and get the owner's permission and any needed approval first

quiz.q: During a debate, someone says 'You only think that because you are young.' What kind of tactic is this?
options: Attacking the person making the point instead of the argument
Using evidence, such as a statistic or a report, to back a point
Asking a clarifying question to understand what the speaker means
Admitting uncertainty about a point when you do not know enough

quiz.q: Your friend wants to change your mind about an issue. Which behaviour shows respectful debate?
options: Interrupting them early so that you can win the argument quickly
Saying that everyone else already agrees with you, so they should give in
Listening, restating their point, then giving your evidence calmly
Walking off and calling them names when they refuse to change their mind

quiz.q: A forwarded message says 'Share to 10 people NOW or something terrible happens' and gives no source. What should you do first?
options: Forward it to 10 people to be safe, in case the warning turns out true
Check whether an official source confirms it before sharing it
Assume it is true because it is urgent and many people seem to be sharing it
Add extra details to make it more convincing before passing it on

quiz.q: Kemi buys 4 cases at 2500 units each, and one is faulty. What is the total paid, and the refund for the faulty one?
options: Total 10000; refund 2500
Total 2500; refund 10000
Total 10000; refund 10000
Total 12500; refund 2500

quiz.q: A coat is marked 8000 units with 15 percent off. What is the price to pay?
options: 1200 units
7985 units
6800 units
9200 units

quiz.q: A caller says they are from your mobile money provider and asks you to read out a one-time code. What should you do?
options: Read out the code, because the caller already knows your name and number
Send the code by text message instead, so that nobody overhears it
Give only half of the code, so the caller cannot use the whole of it
Refuse, hang up and contact the provider through its official number
